title: Prologue (lines 1–114)
focus: the beggar at the sacred grove

teacherSummary.text: Blind and old, Oedipus comes with Antigone at a grove near Athens. A local man tells him it is holy ground of the Eumenides and that he must leave. Oedipus refuses: Apollo foretold that he would end his days here, a blessing to his hosts and a curse to the land that cast him out.

items.prompt: What does Antigone see at the end of the Prologue, and why does Oedipus go silent and step off the public road?
items.expected: She sees “some grey-beards on their way, / Their errand to spy out our resting-place” (lines 109–110). First quit that seat, then question me at large:
The spot thou treadest on is holy ground.
What is the site, to what god dedicate?
Inviolable, untrod; goddesses,
Dread brood of Earth and Darkness, here abide.

anchorPassages.note: Local piety and civic identity meet at the Brass-footed Threshold.
anchorPassages.text:
Whate’er I know thou too shalt know; the place
Is all to great Poseidon consecrate.
Hard by, the Titan, he who bears the torch,
Prometheus, has his worship; but the spot
Thou treadest, the Brass-footed Threshold named,
Is Athens’ bastion, and the neighbouring lands
Claim as their chief and patron yonder knight
Colonus, and in common bear his name.
Such, stranger, is the spot, to fame unknown,
But dear to us its native worshippers.

anchorPassages.note: The oracle of rest, blessing, and curse binds his end to this grove.
anchorPassages.text:
Stern-visaged queens, since coming to this land
First in your sanctuary I bent the knee,
Frown not on me or Phoebus, who, when erst
He told me all my miseries to come,
Spake of this respite after many years,
Some haven in a far-off land, a rest
Vouchsafed at last by dread divinities.
“There,” said he, “shalt thou round thy weary life,
A blessing to the land wherein thou dwell’st,
But to the land that cast thee forth, a curse.”
And of my weird he promised signs should come,
Earthquake, or thunderclap, or lightning flash.
And now I recognise as yours the sign
That led my wanderings to this your grove;
Else had I never lighted on you first,
A wineless man on you who loathe the grape,
Or set me on your seat of native rock.

items.answerGuidance: The stranger says the place is consecrated to Poseidon, that Prometheus is worshipped hard by, and that the neighbouring lands take their name from the knight Colonus. “The place / Is all to great Poseidon consecrate,” he tells Oedipus, then adds that “the neighbouring lands / Claim as their chief and patron yonder knight / Colonus, and in common bear his name.” The grove of the goddesses therefore sits inside a named Attic deme, not in a blank wilderness.

items.text: Why does Oedipus refuse to leave the grove once he hears it is holy ground?
items.lookFor: He refuses because he recognises the grove as the resting place Apollo foretold. After the stranger names the “Dread brood of Earth and Darkness,” Oedipus answers, “Then may they show their suppliant grace, for I / From this your sanctuary will ne’er depart.” The refusal is not stubbornness for its own sake: he takes the holiness of the spot as the “watchword of my fate,” the sign that his wandering has reached the haven promised him.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: He refuses because he recognises the grove as the resting place Apollo foretold. After the stranger names the “Dread brood of Earth and Darkness,” Oedipus answers, “Then may they show their suppliant grace, for I / From this your sanctuary will ne’er depart.” The refusal is not stubbornness for its own sake: he takes the holiness of the spot as the “watchword of my fate,” the sign that his wandering has reached the haven promised him.

items.text: Why does Oedipus want the stranger to summon Theseus, even though he is a sightless beggar?
items.lookFor: He believes his coming can help the king, and that “The blind man’s words will be instinct with sight.” When the stranger asks, “How can he profit from a sightless man?” Oedipus answers with that claim, then asks that “a slight service may avail him much.” The request shows that Oedipus already understands his coming as a political gift to Athens, not merely as a plea for food and rest.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: He believes his coming can help the king, and that “The blind man’s words will be instinct with sight.” When the stranger asks, “How can he profit from a sightless man?” Oedipus answers with that claim, then asks that “a slight service may avail him much.” The request shows that Oedipus already understands his coming as a political gift to Athens, not merely as a plea for food and rest.

items.text: What does “Prologue (lines 1–114)” suggest about the beggar at the sacred grove? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: An inference that the beggar is more than helpless: he asks for little, yet he already treats this grove as the rest Apollo promised him, so weakness and authority sit side by side.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Oedipus’s poverty hides a sense of purpose. He says “’Tis little that he craves, / And less obtains—that less enough for me” (lines 4–5), yet once he hears the ground is holy he announces that he “From this your sanctuary will ne’er depart” (line 45). The beggar who needs a guide also believes the gods have brought him to this exact spot.

items.text: Find one example of setting in “Prologue (lines 1–114)”. What does it reveal about the beggar at the sacred grove that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: One concrete detail of place, such as the “Brass-footed Threshold” or the laurel, olive and nightingales, explained for what it shows: the ground he rests on is holy and guarded, so his resting place is a public matter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The stranger tells him that “the spot / Thou treadest, the Brass-footed Threshold named, / Is Athens’ bastion” (lines 57–59). The rock a blind beggar sits on is also a guard-post of the city. A plain statement would say only that he is trespassing; the setting shows that where he chooses to rest touches the safety of the whole city.

items.text: How does the characterization in “Prologue (lines 1–114)” shape what we understand about the beggar at the sacred grove?
items.lookFor: How Oedipus’s words and the stranger’s reaction build a double portrait: a man humbled by suffering who still speaks like a king, and whom even a hostile local judges “noble.”
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Oedipus says he is “taught by suffering to endure” (line 6), but within minutes he is asking for the lord of Athens, claiming that “a slight service may avail him much” (line 72). The stranger, who wants him off the seat, still says “by thy looks, marred though they be by fate, / I judge thee noble” (lines 76–77). The characterization makes the beggar someone to be reckoned with, not only pitied.

items.text: In the passage that opens with “Child of an old…”, why might Sophocles have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Two words from lines 1–13, each with its connotation, and what the pair shows together, for example “scanted dole” (a stingy handout), “wanderer” (no home), “nobility” (rank kept in ruin) or “denizens” (locals whose rules he must obey).
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The phrase “scanted dole” (line 3) makes his food a grudging handout, so we feel how far a king has fallen. The word “nobility” (line 8) pushes back: suffering, time “And last not least, by true nobility” have taught him to endure, so he claims an inner rank that poverty cannot take. Together the words present a man who is poor in goods but not in dignity.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Prologue (lines 1–114)”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The turn is the stranger’s news that the ground belongs to the dread goddesses. Oedipus hears it as a sign and refuses to move, so the local men must be fetched to decide.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The turn comes when the stranger says the spot belongs to the “Dread brood of Earth and Darkness” (line 40). Instead of leaving, Oedipus calls this “The watchword of my fate” (line 47). Because he will not move, the stranger goes for the local men, who “will soon decide / Whether thou art to rest or go thy way” (lines 79–80). The next scene will have to be a confrontation.

items.text: As the opening scene, what does “Prologue (lines 1–114)” set up that the rest of Oedipus at Colonus will need?
items.lookFor: What the opening plants for the whole play: Apollo’s promise of rest, a blessing to the hosts and a curse to the land that cast him out (lines 91–93), the promised signs (lines 94–95), and the open question of whether this land will take him in.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The Prologue sets up the promise the rest of the play tests. Apollo said Oedipus would “round thy weary life, / A blessing to the land wherein thou dwell’st, / But to the land that cast thee forth, a curse” (lines 91–93), and “promised signs should come” (line 94). From here the audience watches for two things: whether this land will receive him, and when the promised signs will appear.

items.text: In “Prologue (lines 1–114)”, what can we infer about a character's motives from what they say on stage about the beggar at the sacred grove, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: A motive read beneath a stated claim, for example the stranger, who claims only to follow procedure but is afraid to act alone on holy ground, or Oedipus, who promises silence but is gathering information.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The stranger says only that “’tis not mine to bid thee hence without / Due warrant and instruction from the State” (lines 48–49); beneath the rule-following, he is wary of acting alone on holy ground and hands the decision up. Oedipus says he will “be mute” (line 111), but his reason is tactical: “A prudent man / Will ever shape his course by what he learns” (lines 113–114). His silence is a way of reading his judges before he speaks.

items.text: Go back to the bell-ringer question (What does a community owe a stranger it fears?). Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised bell-ringer answer that changes because of a specific Prologue line, such as the stranger’s wish to see him “out of harm” or Oedipus’s plea that Athens “pity this dishonoured shade.”
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: My first answer was that a community owes a stranger safety. Now I would say it owes him at least a fair hearing before it acts. Even the stranger who wants him off the holy seat says, “I fain would see thee out of harm” (line 75), and lets the local men decide instead of acting alone. Oedipus’s prayer, “Athens, first / Of cities, pity this dishonoured shade” (lines 106–107), shows what he hopes that hearing will bring.

items.text: Is Oedipus a helpless beggar or a man still in control in the Prologue? Defend your view with evidence from this section.
items.lookFor: A clear position weighed against the other side: helplessness (he needs Antigone to guide “these dark steps”) against control (he refuses to move, asks for the king, and reads the sign for himself).
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: he is helpless in body but in control of the scene. He cannot walk alone (“Guide these dark steps and seat me there secure,” line 21), yet he decides what happens next by refusing to leave the grove and asking, “Might one be sent from you to summon him?” (line 70). Counter-line: his prayer, “Grant me some consummation of my life, / If haply I appear not all too vile” (lines 102–103), shows he knows his fate still lies with others.

items.text: Consider this reading of the scene (a claim, not a line from the text): The king who once solved riddles must now ask where he is. The forbidden grove of the Furies becomes his place of rest. How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A stand on both halves of the reading: the reversal (the man who must ask where he is) and the forbidden grove as his rest. A careful answer notes that this translation never names the Furies or a riddle, so that part depends on outside knowledge.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: agree, with a qualification. Oedipus opens by asking, “What region, say, whose city have we reached?” (line 2), so a man famous for knowing must depend on others even for where he is. He treats the forbidden ground as his promised haven: “now I recognise as yours the sign / That led my wanderings to this your grove” (lines 96–97). The qualification is that the text calls the goddesses “The Gracious Ones” (line 42), and the riddle belongs to the earlier story, so students should mark which part of the claim comes from outside the scene.

items.text: Which character in “Prologue (lines 1–114)” acts most wisely in the matter of the beggar at the sacred grove, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: A named standard, such as prudence (acting only on what you know), applied to two characters in the Prologue, with a line for each and a reason the other falls short.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: by the standard of prudence, the stranger acts most wisely. He warns that “The spot thou treadest on is holy ground” (line 37) but will not expel Oedipus without the State’s word. Antigone is close behind, since she scouts the land and finds “a man hard by” to ask (line 29). By the same standard Oedipus acts least wisely, staking everything on his reading of a sign. A student could argue the reverse, though, because he too waits “Till I have learned their drift” (line 113).

items.text: You are directing “Prologue (lines 1–114)”. Make two staging choices (a line delivery, a movement, a light or sound cue) and explain how each shapes the audience's view of the beggar at the sacred grove.
items.lookFor: Two staging choices tied to particular lines, each with its effect on how the audience sees the beggar: for example his stillness on the rock, a change of light for the prayer, or Antigone guiding him into hiding.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: (1) Hold Oedipus seated and still on a central rock while the stranger stands over him on “First quit that seat, then question me at large” (line 36). The stillness makes his refusal look like a choice, not frailty. (2) After the stranger leaves, narrow the light to one warm pool and have Oedipus kneel for “Hear, gentle daughters of primeval Night” (line 105). The audience sees a ruined man addressing the powers of the place almost as an equal. Both choices let the beggar command a stage he cannot see.

items.text: Write your own questions about “Prologue (lines 1–114)”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions, each answerable from lines 1–114: one recall, one why/how and one should/what-if, not three versions of the same question.
followUps: Which of your questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Model set. Recall: To whom does the stranger say the grove belongs? (The “Dread brood of Earth and Darkness,” line 40.) Why/how: Why does Oedipus call the holiness of the spot “The watchword of my fate” (line 47)? (He takes it as Apollo’s promised sign.) Should/what if: Should the stranger have expelled him at once? (Answers weigh the sanctity of the ground against the stranger’s choice to wait for “Due warrant and instruction from the State,” line 49.)

items.text: Connect “Prologue (lines 1–114)”, with its focus on the beggar at the sacred grove, to curse and mercy: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Sophocles need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment about curse and mercy, the theme the question names. Mercy is asked for and a curse is announced, but no one has yet granted either. A strong answer names what Sophocles must show next: the people of this place choosing mercy or refusing it.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the link is strong in words but untested in action. Mercy is asked for (“Then may they show their suppliant grace,” line 44; “pity this dishonoured shade,” line 107), and a curse is promised to “the land that cast thee forth” (line 93). But no one in the Prologue grants mercy; the stranger only postpones a decision. To strengthen the link, Sophocles would need to show the local people deciding whether to show mercy to a stranger whose name they do not yet know.

items.text: Is the setting in “Prologue (lines 1–114)” effective in presenting the beggar at the sacred grove, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: A judgment of the grove setting against a stated criterion (does it drive the conflict, or only decorate?), with one detail that meets the criterion and one that might miss it.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: effective, because the setting is the conflict. The beauty Antigone describes, “surely holy ground; / A wilderness of laurel, olive, vine” (lines 16–17), invites rest, while the same ground is “Inviolable, untrod” (line 39), so every detail pushes him both to stay and to leave. Counter-line: the stranger’s list of Poseidon, Prometheus and the knight Colonus (lines 54–61) can read like a guidebook. A reviewer might call it heavy-handed unless the class sees how it ties the local people to their place.

items.text: Compare how “Prologue (lines 1–114)” treats the beggar at the sacred grove with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Oedipus at Colonus see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A named comparison (a play, film or real situation of someone seeking shelter or asylum) and one thing the Prologue sees that the other misses, tied to a line.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Many modern stories about asylum seekers focus on the host country’s rules. The Prologue notices something they often miss: the newcomer comes with his own sense of purpose and worth. Oedipus is a beggar, yet he insists, “The blind man’s words will be instinct with sight” (line 74). He expects to give as well as receive. A strong answer names its comparison exactly and says what each one notices.

items.text: Predict what “Parodos (lines 115–248)” will bring, using two clues from this scene. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction built on two clues from the end of the Prologue, the grey-beards coming “to spy out our resting-place” and the warning that the locals “will soon decide,” then checked after reading.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Clue 1: Antigone sees “some grey-beards on their way, / Their errand to spy out our resting-place” (lines 109–110), so the next scene will probably open as a search. Clue 2: the stranger said they “will soon decide / Whether thou art to rest or go thy way” (lines 79–80), so it should end in a judgment on whether he may stay. A sharper prediction also asks what will happen once the locals hear the name he has not yet given them.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of “Prologue (lines 1–114)” (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about the beggar at the sacred grove?
items.lookFor: An adaptation that holds the core situation: a disgraced, dependent outsider sits on protected ground and claims a right to stay. It names two details that must survive, such as a guide who sees for him or a local who will not decide alone.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: A disgraced former official, now blind and poor, is led by his teenage daughter into a fenced memorial garden in a capital city and sits down inside it. A gardener tells him to leave. He refuses, saying he was told long ago that he would find rest here, and asks to speak to the mayor. Two things must stay: his dependence on the daughter who sees for him (“her whose eyes / Must serve both her and me,” lines 33–34), and the protected status of the ground, which turns his rest into a public question.
